clarissa harlowe or the history of a young lady nine volumes volume i
clarissa or the history of a young lady comprehending the most important concerns of private life
and particularly shew the distresses that may attend the misconduct both of parents and child in relation to marriage
preface the follow history be give in a series of letter write principally in a double yet separate correspondence between two young lady of virtue and honor bear an inviolable friendship for each other and write not merely for amusement but upon the most interesting subject in which every private family more or less may find itself concern and between two gentleman of free life one of they glory in his talent for stratagem and invention and communicate to the other in confidence all the secret purpose of an intriguing head and resolute heart
but here it will be proper to observe for the sake of such as may apprehend hurt to the moral of youth from the more freely-write letter that the gentleman though profess libertine as to the female sex and make it one of their wicked maxim to keep no faith with any of the individual of it who be throw into their power be not however either infidel or scoffer nor yet such as think themselves free from the observance of those other moral duty which bind man to man
on the contrary it will be find in the progress of the work that they very often make such reflection upon each other and each upon himself and his own action as reasonable being must make who disbelieve not a future state of reward and punishment and who one day propose to reform--one of they actually reform and by that mean give an opportunity to censure the freedom which fall from the gayer pen and light heart of the other
and yet that other although in unbosom himself to a select friend he discover wickedness enough to entitle he to general detestation preserve a decency as well in his image as in his language which be not always to be find in the work of some of the most celebrated modern writer whose subject and character have less warrant the liberty they have take
in the letter of the two young lady it be presume will be find not only the high exercise of a reasonable and practicable friendship between mind endow with the noble principle of virtue and religion but occasionally intersperse such delicacy of sentiment particularly with regard to the other sex such instance of impartiality each freely as a fundamental principle of their friendship blame praise and set right the other as be strongly to be recommend to the observation of the young part more specially of female reader
the principle of these two young lady be propose as an exemplar to her sex
nor be it any objection to she be so that she be not in all respect a perfect character
it be not only natural but it be necessary that she should have some fault be it only to show the reader how laudably she could mistrust and blame herself and carry to her own heart divest of self-partiality the censure which arise from her own conviction and that even to the acquittal of those because revere character whom no one else would acquit and to whose much great fault her error be owe and not to a weak or reproachable heart
as far as it be consistent with human frailty and as far as she could be perfect consider the people she have to deal with and those with whom she be inseparably connect she be perfect
to have be impeccable must have leave nothing for the divine grace and a purified state to do and carry our idea of she from woman to angel
as such be she often esteem by the man whose heart be so corrupt that he could hardly believe human nature capable of the purity which on every trial or temptation shine out in she s sic
besides the four principal person several other be introduce whose letter be characteristic and it be presume that there will be find in some of they but more especially in those of the chief character among the man and the second character among the woman such stroke of gayety fancy and humour as will entertain and divert and at the same time both warn and instruct
all the letter be write while the heart of the writer must be suppose to be wholly engage in their subject the event at the time generally dubious so that they abound not only in critical situation but with what may be call instantaneous description and reflection proper to be bring home to the breast of the youthful reader as also with affect conversation many of they write in the dialogue or dramatic way
much more lively and affect say one of the principal character must be the style of those who write in the height of a present distress the mind torture by the pang of uncertainty the event then hide in the womb of fate than the dry narrative unanimated style of a person relate difficulty and danger surmount can be the relater perfectly at ease and if himself unmove by his own story not likely greatly to affect the reader what will be find to be more particularly aim at in the follow work be--to warn the inconsiderate and thoughtless of the one sex against the base art and design of specious contriver of the other to caution parent against the undue exercise of their natural authority over their child in the great article of marriage-- to warn child against prefer a man of pleasure to a man of probity upon that dangerous but too-commonly-receive notion that a reform rake make the good husband--but above all to investigate the high and most important doctrine not only of morality but of christianity by show they throw into action in the conduct of the worthy character while the unworthy who set those doctrine at defiance be condignly and as may be say consequentially punish
from what have be say considerate reader will not enter upon the perusal of the piece before they as if it be design only to divert and amuse
it will probably be think tedious to all such as dip into it expect a light novel or transitory romance and look upon story in it interesting as that be generally allow to be as its sole end rather than as a vehicle to the instruction
different person as might be expect have be of different opinion in relation to the conduct of the heroine in particular situation and several worthy person have object to the general catastrophe and other part of the history
whatever be think material of these shall be take notice of by way of postscript at the conclusion of the history for this work be address to the public as a history of life and manner those part of it which be propose to carry with they the force of an example ought to be as unobjectionable as be consistent with the design of the whole and with human nature

letter iv miss cl
harlowe to antony harlowe esq

honoured sir i be very sorry for my pert letter to my uncle harlowe
yet i do not intend it to be pert
people new to misfortune may be too easily move to impatience
the fall of a regular person no doubt be dreadful and inexcusable
be like the sin of apostacy
would to heaven however that i have have the circumstance of mine inquire into
if sir i make myself bad than i be in my health and well than i be in my penitence it be fit i should be punish for my double dissimulation and you have the pleasure of be one of my punisher
my sincerity in both respect will however be well justify by the event
to that i refer may heaven give you always as much comfort in reflect upon the reprobation i have meet with as you seem to have pleasure in mortify a young creature extremely mortify and that from a right sense as she presume to hope of her own fault
what you hear of i i cannot tell
when the near and dear relation give up an unhappy wretch it be not to be wonder at that those who be not related to she be ready to take up and propagate slander against she
yet i think i may defy calumny itself and except the fatal though involuntary step of april 10 wrap myself in my own innocence and be easy
i thank you sir nevertheless for your caution mean it what it will
as to the question require of i to answer and which be allow to be too shocking either for a mother to put to a daughter or a sister to a sister and which however you say i must answer o sir and must i answer this then be my answer a little time a much less time than be imagine will afford a more satisfactory answer to my whole family and even to my brother and sister than i can give in word nevertheless be pleased to let it be remember that i do not petition for a restoration to favour
i could not hope for that
nor yet to be put in possession of any part of my own estate
nor even for mean of necessary subsistence from the produce of that estate--but only for a blessing for a last blessing
and this i will far add because it be true that i have no wilful crime to charge against myself no free live at bed and at board as you phrase it
why why sir be not other inquiry make of i as well as this shocking one inquirie that modesty would have permit a mother or sister to make and which if i may be excuse to say so would have be still less improper and more charitable to have be make by uncle be the mother forbid or the sister not incline to make they than those they have make
although my humble application have bring upon i so much severe reproach i repent not that i have write to my mother although i cannot but wish that i have not write to my sister because i have satisfy a dutiful consciousness by it however unanswered by the wish-for success
nevertheless i cannot help say that mine be indeed a hard fate that i cannot beg pardon for my capital error without do it in such term as shall be an aggravation of the offence
but i have well leave off lest as my full mind i find be rise to my pen i have other pardon to beg as i multiply line where none at all will be give
god almighty bless preserve and comfort my dear sorrowing and grievously offend father and mother and continue in honour favour and merit my happy sister may god forgive my brother and protect he from the violence of his own temper as well as from the destroyer of his sister s honour and may you my dear uncle and your no less now than ever dear brother my second papa as he use to bid i call he be blessed and happy in they and in each other and in order to this may you all speedily banish from your remembrance for ever the unhappy clarissa harlowe

all your friend here my dear young lady now seem set upon propose to you to go to one of the plantation

and can it be that this admirable creature will so soon leave this cursed world
for cursed i shall think it and more cursed myself when she be go
o jack
thou who canst sit so cool and like addison s angel direct and even enjoy the storm that tear up my happiness by the root blame i not for my impatience however unreasonable
if thou know that already i feel the torment of the damned in the remorse that wring my heart on look back upon my past action by she thou wouldst not be the devil thou art to halloo on a worrying conscience which without my merciless aggravation be altogether intolerable
i know not what to write nor what i would write
when the company that use to delight i be as uneasy to i as my reflection be painful and i can neither help nor divert myself must not every servant about i partake in a perturbation so sincere
shall i give thee a faint picture of the horrible uneasiness with which my mind struggle
and faint indeed it must be for nothing but outrageous madness can exceed it and that only in the apprehension of other since as to the sufferer it be certain that actual distraction take it out of its lucid interval must be an infinitely more happy state than the state of suspense and anxiety which often bring it on
forbid to attend the dear creature yet long to see she i would give the world to be admit once more to her beloved presence
i ride towards london three or four time a day resolve pro and con twenty time in two or three mile and at last ride back and in view of uxbridge loathe even the kind friend and hospitable house turn my horse s head again towards the town and resolve to gratify my humour let she take it as she will but at the very entrance of it after infinite canvassing once more alter my mind dread to offend and shock she lest by that mean i should curtail a life so precious
yesterday in particular to give you an idea of the strength of that impatience which i cannot avoid suffer to break out upon my servant i have no soon dispatch will than i take horse to meet he on his return
in order to give he time i loiter about on the road rid up this lane to the one highway down that to the other just as my horse point all the way curse my very being and though so lately look down upon all the world wish to change condition with the poor beggar that cry to i for charity as i ride by he--and throw he money in hope to obtain by his prayer the blessing my heart pant after
after i have saunter about an hour or two which seem three or four tedious one fear i have slipt the fellow i inquire at every turnpike whether a servant in such a livery have not pass through in his return from london on a full gallop for woe have be to the dog have i meet he on a sluggish trot
and lest i should miss he at one end of kensingtohn as he might take either the acton or hammersmith road or at the other as he might come through the park or not how many score time do i ride backwards and forwards from the palace to the gore make myself the subject of observation to all passenger whether on horseback or on foot who no doubt wonder to see a well-dress and well-mount man sometimes amble sometimes prance as the beast have more fire than his master backwards and forwards in so short a compass
yet all this time though long to espy the fellow do i dread to meet he lest he should be charge with fatal tiding
when at distance i see any man gallop towards i my resemblance-form fancy immediately make it to be he and then my heart choke i
but when the person s near approach undeceive i how do i curse the varlet s delay and thee by turn
and how ready be i to draw my pistol at the stranger for have the impudence to gallop which none but my messenger i think have either right or reason to do
for all the business of the world i be ready to imagine should stand still on an occasion so melancholy and so interesting to i
nay for this week past i could cut the throat of any man or woman i see laugh while i be in such dejection of mind
i be now convinced that the wretch who fly from a heavy scene labour under ten time more distress in the intermediate suspense and apprehension than they could have be they present at it and to see and know the bad so capable be fancy or imagination the more immediate offspring of the soul to outgo fact let the subject be either joyous or grievous
and hence as i conceive it be that all pleasure be great in the expectation or in the reflection than in fruition as all pain which press heavy upon both part of that unequal union by which frail mortality hold its precarious tenure be ever most acute in the time of suffering for how easy sit upon the reflection the heavy misfortune when surmounted but most easy i confess those in which body have more concern than soul
this however be a point of philosophy i have neither time nor head just now to weigh so take it as it fall from a madman s pen
woe be to either of the wretch who shall bring i the fatal news that she be no more
for it be but too likely that a shriek-owl so hat will never hoot or scream again unless the shock that will probably disorder my whole frame on so sad an occasion by unsteadye my hand shall divert my aim from his head heart or bowel if it turn not against my own
but surely she will not she cannot yet die
such a matchless excellence whose mind contain a world and seem for all thing fram d could not be lend to be so soon demand back again
but may it not be that thou belford art in a plot with the dear creature who will not let i attend she to convince myself in order to work up my soul to the deep remorse and that when she be convinced of the sincerity of my penitence and when my mind be make such wax as to be fit to take what impression she please to give it she will then raise i up with the joyful tiding of her return health and acceptance of i
what would i give to have it so
and when the happiness of hundred as well as the peace and reconciliation of several eminent family depend upon her restoration and happiness why should it not be so
but let i presume it will
let i indulge my former hope however improbable--i will and enjoy it too
and let i tell thee how ecstatic my delight would be on the unravelling of such a plot as this
do dear belford let it be so and o my dearest and ever-dear clarissa keep i no loner in this cruel suspense in which i suffer a thousand time more than ever i make thee suffer
nor fear thou that i will resent or recede on an ecclaircissement so desirable for i will adore thee for ever and without reproach thee for the pang thou hast torture i with confess thee as much my superior in virtue and honour
but once more should the bad happen--say not what that bad be--and i be go from this hat island--go for ever--and may eternal--but i be craze already--and will therefore conclude myself thine more than my own and no great compliment neither r l

sally martin be the daughter of a substantial mercer at the court-end of the town to whom her mother a grocer s daughter in the city bring a handsome fortune and both have a gay turn and be fond of the fashion which it be their business to promote and which the wife and daughter of the uppermost tradesman especially in that quarter of the town generally affect to follow it be no wonder that they bring up their daughter accordingly nor that she who be a very sprightly and ready-witted girl and reckon very pretty and very genteel should every year improve upon such example

this error they have be lead into by a ridiculous doctrine in modern criticism that they be oblige to an equal distribution of reward and punishment and an impartial execution of poetical justice
who be the first that establish this rule i know not but i be sure it have no foundation in nature in reason or in the practice of the antient
we find that good and evil happen alike unto all men on this side the grave and as the principal design of tragedy be to raise commiseration and terror in the mind of the audience we shall defeat this great end if we always make virtue and innocence happy and successful
whatever cross and disappoint a good man suffer in the body of the tragedy they will make but small impression on our mind when we know that in the last act he be to arrive at the end of his wish and desire
when we see he engage in the depth of his affliction we be apt to comfort ourselves because we be sure he will find his way out of they and that his grief however great soever it may be at present will soon terminate in gladness
